chapter: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
title: Mildred's musical insight and speed at learning songs
summary: She quickly recognized good players and learned songs almost instantly, even for record dates with Eddie Sauter arrangements.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Well yeah, I thought -- It was interesting to me to find out, because you know, that's before I knew either of you and you know it's different. Course you -- you were completely wrapped up in music and all that you were doing. But, at the same time, were you -- were you kind of thrilled to -- you know to --
And -- and she -- um -- I mean Mildred was always kind of cool, wasn't she? She was always -- I mean
Mildred was never overwhelmed by anything, was she? You know she was --
-- well, was she at all different then, or what?
She had a very good understanding of music --
She had a real keen insight.
She knew what she could hear --
Oh, yes, but she had a keen insight and she was affected -- anybody that played well, she -- she dug it right away --
-- I don't know what it was --
But she heard -- she heard well. She heard everything.
Yeah. She wasn't fooled, she didn't make mistakes.

-- all her things she had complete control of anything that she did. Yet, it used to amaze me ah -- how easygoing she would go about things. She'd come into a song, she'd say, 'Dave, play it over on the piano.' And she'd put it up and he'd play it over a couple of times, she'd kind of listen to it, listen to it, and she'd do it. It used to amaze me. Even later, when we were working together, we'd have tunes to record, and Eddie Sauter would be writing them, and she'd be getting for the record date, she'd say, yell down and say, 'Play that -- that tune. Play a couple of those tunes.' So da-da-da-da-, this is it, and I'd play the melody. For her. With the harmony. And she'd go right on the date, put the (unintelli-
words up, gible) go through it once, she's ready to record.
